blocks.text: **The problem.** Given a string `s`, return `true` if it can be built by writing one substring two or more times in a row, like `"abcabcabc"` from `"abc"`.

blocks.alt: Two views of abcabcabc. On top, the string split into three blocks, abc, abc, abc. Below, the string written twice in a row, with its first and last letters greyed out. The original string still appears inside, starting at index 3, which only happens for a repeated block. Its longest border, a prefix that is also a suffix, is abcabc, six letters long, so shifting the string by 9 minus 6, or 3, lines it up with itself.

elements.text: s + s, without its first and last letter, still contains s
elements.originalText: s + s, without its first and last letter, still contains s

blocks.code:
s = "abab"         ->  true    ("ab" twice)
s = "aba"          ->  false
s = "abcabcabcabc" ->  true    ("abc" four times, or "abcabc" twice)
s = "abacaba"      ->  false   (starts and ends with "aba", but 7 letters don't split into blocks)

blocks.text: The idea: a repeated string overlaps itself

If `s` is a block `B` written k ≥ 2 times, then dropping the first block or the last block leaves the same string. So `s` has a **border** — a prefix that is also a suffix — of length n - |B|, and shifting `s` by |B| places lines it up with itself. That gives two quick tests: look for `s` inside a doubled copy of itself, or read the longest border from the KMP table.

A border alone isn't enough. `"abacaba"` has the border `"aba"`, so shifting by 4 lines it up — but 4 doesn't divide 7, and the last block would be cut short. The shift has to split the string into **whole blocks**.
A block length must divide n. Try each one up to n / 2, and check whether repeating the first block rebuilds `s`.
**Time O(n · d), space O(n),** where d is the number of divisors of n — each check costs O(n). d is small in practice (at most 2√n), so this is fast enough for most inputs.

Write `s` twice and cut off the first and last letter. If `s` is a repeated block, it still appears inside — starting one block in. If it isn't, the only copies of `s` in `s + s` are at the very start and the very end, and both have been cut.

blocks.code:
def repeated_substring_pattern(s):
    return s in (s + s)[1:-1]             # s must appear somewhere in the middle

blocks.text: **Time O(n) with a linear search such as KMP, space O(n)** for the doubled string. The built-in search is usually fast, but some libraries fall back to O(n²) on unlucky inputs — so say which search you're assuming.

blocks.caption: Build the KMP table for s; the last entry is the longest border, and n minus it is the block length.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n).** Why is the **longest** border the right one to check? It gives the **smallest** shift, and if any block length works, the smallest shift divides it — so testing that one shift is enough.

blocks.alt: Every block length: O(n·d) time, O(n) space. Doubling trick: O(n) time, O(n) space. KMP border: O(n) time, O(n) space.

blocks.text: The doubling trick is linear only with a linear-time search such as KMP. It is the one-liner interviewers like to see explained; the KMP version shows why it runs in linear time.

items: **One letter** — `"a"` is `false`: a block must appear at least twice.
**A border that doesn't fit** — `"abacaba"` and `"aabaaba"` are `false`; forgetting the `n % period` check says `true`.
**Several block lengths** — `"abababab"` works with `"ab"` and `"abab"`; any one is enough.
**Find the First Occurrence in a String** — where the KMP table comes from. Previous lesson.
**Repeated String Match** — how many copies of `a` are needed so that `b` is a substring: repeat until long enough, then one search.
**Rotate String** — is `goal` a rotation of `s`? The same doubling trick: `(s + s).includes(goal)` with equal lengths.
**Longest Happy Prefix** — return the longest border itself: it is `lps[n - 1]`.
